families.outcome: Choose the right function AND give it a range that covers the whole data set
families.context: A canteen's week of sales in B2:B6, with a SUM in B7 whose range starts one row too low

variants.variation: evaluate the formula exactly as written, not as intended
variants.misconception: believes SUM finds the whole column because the label says Total

variants.variation: produce the corrected formula rather than recognise it
variants.misconception: starts the range at the row below the heading without checking where the first value is

variants.variation: diagnose a stated discrepancy of Rs 450 between a displayed total and a hand total
variants.misconception: attributes a wrong total to the function rather than to the range it was given

variants.variation: change one cell OUTSIDE the range and predict the change (zero)
variants.misconception: thinks editing any cell in a column refreshes every total below it

families.outcome: Know exactly what AVERAGE counts, and what an empty cell does to it
families.context: Five pupils' marks with B4 empty because one pupil was absent

variants.variation: evaluate AVERAGE over a range containing a blank
variants.misconception: divides by the number of cells in the range instead of the number of values found

variants.variation: reconcile two formulas that add the same numbers and disagree
variants.misconception: assumes a built-in function and the equivalent hand arithmetic must agree

variants.variation: fill the blank and recompute; the average FALLS although a mark was added
variants.misconception: believes adding a mark always raises an average

variants.variation: name a different function for a different summary of the same range
variants.misconception: confuses reading a value (MAX) with rearranging the data (sorting)

variants.variation: choose the change that makes the sheet follow a stated rule
variants.misconception: thinks a cell that looks filled (a typed space) is filled as far as AVERAGE is concerned

families.outcome: Use COUNTIF and IF with the correct comparison operator and the correct reference type
families.context: Six marks against a pass mark of 50, with one mark sitting exactly on the boundary

variants.variation: count against a >= criterion where one value is exactly on the boundary
variants.misconception: reads >=50 as 'above 50' and drops the pupil who scored exactly 50

variants.variation: identify WHICH record two nearly identical criteria disagree about
variants.misconception: assumes > and >= give the same count

variants.variation: pick the IF whose argument order and comparison both match the rule
variants.misconception: swaps the true/false results, or reverses the comparison so low marks pass

variants.variation: diagnose why a copied IF returns the same word in every row
variants.misconception: believes $ signs make a formula 'safer' rather than fixing one address

variants.variation: name the function that applies a condition, as the family's entry point
variants.misconception: reaches for COUNT or COUNTA, which apply no test at all

families.outcome: Decide which reference in a formula must be absolute before it is copied
families.context: Three item prices and one VAT rate stored once, in B6, below the data

variants.variation: work out which two cells a correctly written formula uses after being copied
variants.misconception: thinks copying a formula copies its result rather than its pattern

variants.variation: resolve two symptoms at once - the first row right, the rows below zero
variants.misconception: trusts a formula because the row it was typed in looks correct

variants.variation: produce the formula, deciding per reference which part must be locked
variants.misconception: locks both references, giving every item the first item's VAT

variants.variation: change the shared rate and predict a dependent cell without retyping anything
variants.misconception: believes a formula must be retyped after the value it refers to changes

families.outcome: Trace a Python loop with a condition, and say what one edit changes
families.context: marks = [45, 62, 38, 71, 50] counted against a pass mark inside a for loop

variants.variation: trace the loop and report the counter
variants.misconception: counts 50 as failing a >= test

variants.variation: change the comparison operator by one character and re-trace
variants.misconception: treats > and >= as interchangeable in code

variants.variation: change the accumulator from +1 to +m, so the variable stops being a count
variants.misconception: does not distinguish a counter from a running total

variants.variation: move print one indentation level and predict the change in behaviour
variants.misconception: treats indentation as layout rather than as the thing that defines a block

variants.variation: count how many times the TEST runs, not how many times it is true
variants.misconception: confuses the number of loop iterations with the number of matches

families.outcome: Dry-run a while loop and reason about the value it stops on
families.context: count = 10 stepping down by 3 while count > 0, with a step counter

variants.variation: count the passes round the loop
variants.misconception: stops the trace at 1 and answers 3, forgetting the condition is tested before a pass

variants.variation: report the final value, which overshoots the limit
variants.misconception: believes a loop stops the instant its variable reaches the limit

variants.variation: judge a pupil's claim that the program is buggy
variants.misconception: assumes an unexpected result must be a coding error rather than the arithmetic of the step

variants.variation: reverse the problem - find the starting value that produces a required ending value
variants.misconception: treats the starting value as free when the step size constrains it

families.outcome: Dry-run a flowchart with a loop, and say what each structural change does
families.context: An inline-SVG flowchart: INPUT N, T = 0, C = 1, loop while C <= N adding C to T, OUTPUT T

variants.variation: dry-run to the final output for N = 5
variants.misconception: stops the trace at C = 4 because the last pass is easy to miss

variants.variation: change the decision from <= to < and re-run
variants.misconception: the off-by-one - assumes the loop body count is unaffected by the operator

variants.variation: generalise from one trace to what the algorithm computes for any N
variants.misconception: reads a loop by its counter instead of by the box inside it

variants.variation: swap the two boxes inside the loop and re-run
variants.misconception: believes the order of statements inside a loop does not matter

variants.variation: name the symbol shape, as the family's accessible entry point
variants.misconception: confuses the decision diamond with the process rectangle or the I/O parallelogram

families.outcome: Read a query-by-example grid against a table and predict exactly what it returns
families.context: A six-record LIBRARY table and a QBE grid with Category and Year criteria

variants.variation: apply two criteria on the SAME row (AND) and count the result
variants.misconception: reads >2019 as 'from 2019 onward' and includes the 2019 record

variants.variation: identify the record that satisfies one criterion but is excluded by the other
variants.misconception: filters on the field read first and accepts a record without testing the second

variants.variation: move one criterion to the Or row and count again - the result WIDENS
variants.misconception: believes the grid can only narrow a result set

variants.variation: separate what Show does from what Criteria does
variants.misconception: thinks a field must be displayed in order to be filtered on

variants.variation: name the row that carries the test, as the family's entry point
variants.misconception: confuses the Criteria row with the Field, Table, Show or Sort rows

families.outcome: Distinguish full, incremental and differential backups by what each copies AND by what a restore then costs
families.context: A school office: a full backup every Sunday and one further backup each weeknight

variants.variation: name the method whose starting point is always the last FULL backup
variants.misconception: the exact error in the existing g9ict-esv-042 - calling this incremental

variants.variation: name the method whose starting point moves forward each night
variants.misconception: believes the two methods differ on Monday, when in fact they are identical then

variants.variation: count the sets a differential restore actually needs
variants.misconception: assumes every backup taken during the week must be restored

variants.variation: change one condition (incremental instead of differential) and recount
variants.misconception: does not connect the smaller nightly copy to the longer restore chain

variants.variation: resolve a disagreement in which both sides state something true
variants.misconception: judges a backup plan by how long the backup takes rather than by how reliably it restores

families.outcome: Work with storage capacity, converting units and separating what is used from what remains
families.context: A 32 GB memory card, 8 MB photographs, and a 4 GB video already on it

variants.variation: convert one capacity between units
variants.misconception: divides instead of multiplying when moving to the smaller unit

variants.variation: divide, but only after putting both quantities in the same unit
variants.misconception: divides 32 by 8 and answers 4 - a mixed-unit division

variants.variation: diagnose a stated (and arithmetically correct) claim that rests on a false premise
variants.misconception: total capacity versus space remaining

variants.variation: carry out the corrected calculation the previous variant only described
variants.misconception: converts first and then forgets to subtract the space already used

variants.variation: identify the missing information before any calculation is possible
variants.misconception: treats the facts a situation happens to supply as the facts a calculation needs

families.outcome: Use the pattern of who can and cannot connect to locate a fault in a star network
families.context: An inline-SVG diagram of four lab PCs on a switch, a router and the Internet

variants.variation: read the topology off the diagram
variants.misconception: confuses a star with a bus because both look like 'one line of computers'

variants.variation: one machine fails - eliminate every shared component
variants.misconception: blames a shared device that the three working machines are visibly using

variants.variation: two symptoms that look contradictory - local sharing works, the web does not
variants.misconception: treats 'the network is down' as one thing instead of two layers

variants.variation: remove the central device and count how many machines still reach the Internet
variants.misconception: believes a star is fault-tolerant, missing its single point of failure

variants.variation: compare star and bus on the property of being diagnosable
variants.misconception: judges a topology only by cost or speed, not by what a fault does to it

families.outcome: Decide what an online transaction actually requires, and what a security indicator does and does not promise
families.context: Mrs Ramdin paying an electricity bill online from three different places

variants.variation: given a full inventory of what she HAS, name what is missing
variants.misconception: assumes owning the hardware means holding the service (the corrected form of the audit's g9ict-int-202-a)

variants.variation: evaluate a claim that one safeguard removes all risk
variants.misconception: reads a padlock as sufficient rather than necessary security

variants.variation: produce the protocol name instead of recognising it
variants.misconception: does not distinguish HTTP from HTTPS when entering card details

variants.variation: compare two routes and pick the factor that actually separates them
variants.misconception: chooses a true statement about one option that is irrelevant to the decision

families.outcome: Predict the output of a mail merge from its data source, its main document and its filter
families.context: Four fee-letter recipients and a main document with four merge fields

variants.variation: count the letters a completed merge produces
variants.misconception: counts merge fields instead of records

variants.variation: produce the text one named field prints for one named record
variants.misconception: believes a field prints the same text wherever it appears

variants.variation: diagnose letters that still show the field names after printing
variants.misconception: judges a field by how it looks on screen rather than by whether the program recognises it

variants.variation: add a filter to the recipient list and recount
variants.misconception: thinks the data source must be edited to write to a subset of it

variants.variation: name the two inputs a merge requires
variants.misconception: confuses an output of the process (labels, envelopes) with an input to it

families.outcome: Eliminate causes from evidence, test the cheapest hypothesis first, and change one thing at a time
families.context: A desktop showing No signal while its fan runs and the monitor's own menu still opens

variants.variation: use one observation to rule a cause OUT rather than to pick a cause
variants.misconception: jumps to the most familiar cause instead of narrowing the list

variants.variation: order candidate actions by cost and reversibility
variants.misconception: assumes a dramatic symptom implies a dramatic cause

variants.variation: name what is left after substitution has cleared two of three components
variants.misconception: keeps suspecting a part that has been proved good on another machine

variants.variation: criticise a method rather than solve the fault
variants.misconception: believes fixing the symptom and identifying the fault are the same outcome

families.outcome: Compare a system panel against a stated set of minimum requirements
families.context: An About this PC panel for LAB-PC-07 beside the minimum requirements for LabDraw 12

variants.variation: read one value from the panel - the family's deliberate L1 anchor
variants.misconception: confuses installed RAM with disk space

variants.variation: find the requirement the document CANNOT answer
variants.misconception: assumes a panel titled About this PC describes everything about the machine (the corrected form of the audit's g9ict-sys-204-c, whose answer was printed in the panel)

variants.variation: adjudicate a pupil's claim that rests on a decimal comparison
variants.misconception: reads 1.60 as smaller than 1.5 because 60 is larger than 5

variants.variation: compute the shortfall rather than restate the requirement
variants.misconception: answers 8 - treats a minimum total as the amount to be added

variants.variation: compare two machines where each is better on one requirement
variants.misconception: treats minimum requirements as a score to be totalled, so a strong figure offsets a weak one

needs.problem: The stem reads 'Which backup method copies only the files that have changed since the last full backup?' and keys 'Incremental backup'. That wording describes a DIFFERENTIAL backup. An incremental backup copies what has changed since the last backup of ANY type. The item's own explanation then contradicts its stem: it says 'since the previous backup (full or incremental)'.
needs.fix: Change the stem to 'Which backup method copies only the files that have changed since the previous backup, whether that was a full or an incremental one?' and leave the keyed answer and the explanation as they are. Do NOT change the answer to 'Differential backup': 'Differential backup' is not currently one of the four options, and the surrounding block (esv-041, esv-043) is built around full versus incremental. The differential/full/incremental distinction is now taught properly by g9ict-fam-009-a and g9ict-fam-009-b, which sit in the same chapter and subsection.

notes: Two figures are inline SVG (a sum-to-N flowchart and a star-topology lab) and every data table uses the existing .q-table / .q-scroll classes from style.css rather than per-cell inline styles — .q-table is a fixed light plate with dark ink, which is what keeps a table legible on the practice chalkboard, and it costs far fewer bytes in the question cache than the per-cell style attributes the older ICT files use. No new question field was invented: the family id is the question id minus its -<variant> suffix.
